questions.q: What does separation of concerns mean for backend code?
questions.explain: The problem with the old BookStore handler was that it did six jobs at once. Separation of concerns gives each piece one job, so you can change one job without reading all the others.
options: Every feature of the app runs in its own separate server
Each piece of code has one job and knows as little as possible about the others
Every function is written and owned by a different developer
The code for each HTTP method is kept in a separate file

questions.q: Which job belongs in a controller?
questions.explain: A controller translates between HTTP and the service. It holds no business rules (those are in the model and the service) and no SQL (that is in a repository).
options: Deciding that an order cannot take more copies than the stock
Running the SQL that saves an order
Turning a request into a service call, and the result into a response
Reading the settings from the environment

questions.q: What does a service like OrderService know about?
questions.explain: A service carries out a use case such as "place an order". Reading place out loud gives the business process: check the amount, find the book, take the copies, record the order. HTTP and SQL stay outside it.
options: Status codes, headers and the request body
The steps and rules of one use case, but not HTTP and not SQL
The SQL tables and their column names
Only how to format money for the response

questions.q: What is a DTO?
questions.explain: A DTO describes only what travels over the network. It is not the model: OrderDto shows the total as text and leaves out userId.
options: A database table object: a class that maps each SQL row to one object in memory
A special kind of middleware that checks every request before the controller runs
A data transfer object: the exact shape that crosses the boundary, like a request body
The domain model that holds the business rules, such as the stock check

questions.q: Where should the rule "an order cannot take more copies than there are in stock" live?
questions.explain: It is a business rule that would be true even without computers, so it belongs in the domain. There it needs no server and no database to test.
options: In the controller, next to the status codes
In the SQL WHERE clause only
In the error-handling middleware
In the domain, as a plain function like takeFromStock

questions.q: A PgliteBookRepository class runs SQL to load and save books. Which layer is it in?
questions.explain: Anything that talks to the outside world (databases, HTTP, e-mail) is infrastructure. It implements a port that the application layer defined.
options: Domain
Application
Infrastructure
It is its own layer, the data layer

questions.q: In this lesson, what is a port?
questions.explain: The application says what it needs ("something that can find a book") as an interface. Infrastructure provides the how by implementing it.
options: The network port number that the HTTP server listens on, such as 3000
An interface the application defines for what it needs, such as BookRepository
A class that copies the data from one database into another one
A middleware that forwards each request on to another service

questions.q: Which import breaks the rule "dependencies point inward"?
questions.explain: Outer code may import inner code, never the other way. The domain (model.ts) imports nothing, so a domain file that imports a database repository breaks the rule.
options: order.controller.ts imports order.service.ts
order.service.ts imports model.ts
memory.repositories.ts imports ports.ts
model.ts imports pglite.repositories.ts

questions.q: Why should the domain be the layer that imports nothing?
questions.explain: Drivers, HTTP libraries and frameworks change often. If the domain imported them, every such change would touch your business rules. With arrows pointing inward, you can swap the database and not one rule changes.
options: Because domain files must stay short, and every import makes them longer
It is the most valuable part and changes least, so outside changes must not reach it
Because TypeScript cannot import files that live in another folder
So the domain code loads and runs faster than the other layers

questions.q: OrderService gets its repositories through its constructor instead of creating them. What is this called?
questions.explain: The service receives what it needs from outside. That is why a test can hand it fake repositories and a real app can hand it PostgreSQL ones.
options: Dependency injection
Inheritance
Middleware
Separation of layers

questions.q: Where does the controller get the userId for a new order?
questions.explain: Anything in the body is chosen by the client, so a user could place orders for someone else. The user id must come from the verified token, as in the auth lesson.
options: From a userId field in the request body
From a query string parameter
From the verified token, never from the body
From the last order in the database

questions.q: Why does PlaceOrderDto contain only bookId and quantity, and no price?
questions.explain: The incoming DTO holds only the fields a client may send. If the price came from the body, anyone could buy a book for one cent. The service computes book.priceCents * quantity itself.
options: To make the JSON shorter
Because TypeScript cannot type money
Because the price is set by middleware
A client must not choose the price; the service takes it from the stored book

questions.q: Why does the controller answer with toOrderDto(order) instead of the Order model itself?
questions.explain: The outgoing DTO is the public contract. It picks the fields clients see and formats them ("25.98"), so renaming a model field does not break anyone.
options: The model can change without breaking clients, and internal fields never leak
Because a model class cannot be turned into JSON by JSON.stringify
Because the controller is not allowed to import anything from the domain
Because a DTO makes the response smaller and faster to send

questions.q: What is the composition root?
questions.explain: Every class receives what it needs, so something must build them all in the right order. That is main.ts, the only file that knows every concrete class.
options: The first class in the domain layer
The folder that holds all the interfaces
The one place that creates every concrete class and connects them
The middleware that runs before all others

questions.q: Where does the lesson turn DomainError("out_of_stock") into the status code 409?
questions.explain: The domain speaks in words ("out of stock"), HTTP speaks in numbers (409). handleErrors is the one place where they meet, so the domain never learns about status codes.
options: In takeFromStock
In OrderService.place
In the repository
In the handleErrors middleware

questions.q: For an error that is not a DomainError, handleErrors answers { error: "internal_error" } with status 500. Why not send error.message?
questions.explain: Domain errors are written for users, so their message is safe to show. An unknown error can carry database or code details; the client gets a generic message and you keep the details in your logs.
options: Because a response with status 500 is not allowed to have a body
An unexpected error's message can reveal internals, such as SQL or file paths, to the client
Because error.message is always empty for errors that are not domain errors
To make the error response easier to translate into other languages

questions.q: Why does loadConfig return Object.freeze({ maxQuantity })?
questions.explain: Settings are read once, checked, and then must stay the same. A frozen object cannot be changed by mistake somewhere deep in the code.
options: Frozen objects use less memory
It is needed to read environment variables
So no code can change a setting while the app runs
So the object can be sent as JSON

questions.q: In the practice, you swap the memory book repository for a PGlite one. Which files change?
questions.explain: The service only knows the BookRepository port. A new class implements it, and main passes that class in. No domain or application file changes: the dependency rule paying off.
options: The model, the service and the controller
Only a new infrastructure file and the composition root
Only the service, which now runs SQL
Every file that imports Book

questions.q: With a real database, "find the book, then save it with less stock" has a gap. What is it, and where is it fixed?
questions.explain: Between the read and the write, another request can read the same stock. The fix (one SQL statement, or a transaction) stays in infrastructure, so the service and domain stay the same.
options: The book record may be too large to load at once; fix it in the controller
JSON cannot hold the stock number safely; fix it in the outgoing DTO
Two customers can both read "1 left"; fix it in the repository or with a transaction
The stock may become negative; fix it in the error-handling middleware

questions.q: Why can a test pass two plain objects to new OrderService(books, orders, 10) instead of real repositories?
questions.explain: The service cannot tell a fake from a database: it only calls find, save and add. Any object with those methods fits the port.
options: Because the test file turns off TypeScript's type checks for the service
The service only depends on the port interfaces, and the plain objects satisfy them
Because plain objects are turned into repository classes automatically
Because the service skips its repositories when it runs inside a test

questions.q: What is the main cost of the layered design, according to the lesson?
questions.explain: Wiring dozens of services by hand, in order, with their settings and shutdown, becomes a lot of work. That is the job the next lesson hands to a framework.
options: The business rules can no longer be tested
The app becomes slower at runtime
The database can no longer be changed
More files, and a composition root that grows with every class

questions.explain: The error passes straight through log, so its log line never runs; handleErrors catches it outside. That is why the lesson puts log outermost: then it also logs the failed requests.

questions.q: Finish takeFromStock. If quantity is more than book.stock, throw an Error with the message Only N left (N is the stock). Otherwise return a new book with less stock, and do not change the original.
questions.explain: Check the rule first and throw, then return { ...book, stock: book.stock - quantity }. The spread makes a copy, so the original book keeps its stock of 4.

questions.q: Finish parseReviewDto. Return { bookId, stars } only when body is an object, bookId is a positive whole number, and stars is a whole number from 1 to 5. Otherwise return undefined. Drop every other field.
questions.explain: Check the body is an object and not null, then check each field's type and range. Build a new object with only the allowed fields, so the client's userId never gets through.

questions.q: Finish toOrderDto. It returns { id, quantity, total }, where total is the price in cents as text with two decimals (1299 → "12.99"). It must not include userId or totalCents.
questions.explain: Pick the public fields one by one instead of spreading the whole model. Divide the cents by 100 and use toFixed(2) to get the text "25.98".

questions.q: Finish use(handler, ...middlewares). It wraps the handler so the first middleware is the outermost one. A middleware takes the next handler and returns a new handler.
questions.explain: Build from the inside out: start with the handler and wrap it with the last middleware first. reduceRight walks the list from the end, so the first middleware ends up outermost.

questions.q: Finish the handleErrors middleware. If next throws a DomainError, answer { status, body: { error: code } } with the status from STATUS (use 400 when the code is not in it). Any other error becomes { status: 500, body: { error: "internal_error" } }.
questions.explain: Use return await next(request) inside try, or a rejected promise escapes the catch. Unknown errors get a generic 500 body, so internal details like "db down" never reach the client.

questions.q: Finish loadConfig(env). Read PAGE_SIZE (default "20" when missing). It must be a whole number from 1 to 100, otherwise throw an Error with the message PAGE_SIZE must be 1 to 100. Return a frozen object { pageSize }.
questions.explain: Convert once with Number, check with Number.isInteger (false for NaN and 2.5) and the range, then freeze. A bad setting stops the app at startup.

questions.q: Finish MemoryBookRepository. The constructor stores the given books in a Map by id. find(id) returns the book or undefined, and save(book) stores it (replacing the old one).
questions.explain: A Map keyed by id makes both jobs one line: get returns undefined for an unknown id, and set replaces the old book.

questions.q: Finish place in OrderService: find the book (throw Error("no_such_book") if missing), throw Error("out_of_stock") if quantity is more than its stock, save the book with less stock, and return orders.add({ userId, bookId, quantity, totalCents }). The test uses fake repositories.
questions.explain: The service only calls find, save and add, so plain objects work as repositories. The total comes from the stored price, never from the client.

questions.q: Finish place(request) in the controller. No request.userId: answer { status: 401 }. request.body.quantity not a positive whole number: { status: 400 }. Otherwise call service.place(request.userId, quantity) and answer { status: 201, body: result }. Take the user from request.userId, never from the body.
questions.explain: The controller stays thin: check the user, check the input, call the service, shape the answer. The userId: 1 in the body is ignored; the order belongs to the logged-in user 3.

questions.q: Finish logRequests(log). It returns a middleware that calls the next handler, then calls log with the text user ID -> STATUS, using - when there is no userId, and returns the response.
questions.explain: A middleware is a function that takes next and returns a new handler. Because log is injected, a test can collect the lines in an array instead of printing them.
